summary: Extends SDP capability negotiation with media capabilities, so endpoints can negotiate media types and their parameters, not just transport protocols and attributes. It updates earlier SDP capability negotiation work.

eli5.summary: Before a video chat, both sides list what they can handle and choose something both like, such as a type of picture or sound.

questions: what is sdp media capabilities negotiation
how do endpoints negotiate codecs in sdp
what is the sdp rmcap attribute
what is a latent configuration in sdp
what is the sdp sescap attribute
what does med-v0 mean in sdp
subtitle: Lets two endpoints offer and negotiate codecs, codec settings and even future media streams inside a single SDP exchange.

tldr.problem: The base SDP capability negotiation framework (RFC 5939) can only negotiate transport protocols and attributes. It has no good way to offer alternative codecs and their parameters, or to announce support for a media stream that is not offered yet.
tldr.mechanism: New SDP attributes (rmcap, omcap, mfcap, mscap) describe media formats and their parameters as numbered capabilities. Potential configurations (pcfg) offer them for immediate use, latent configurations (lcfg) announce streams for later, and session capabilities (sescap) say which combinations are acceptable.
tldr.outcome: One offer/answer exchange can settle codecs and their parameters, and the answer reports the chosen configuration in an acfg attribute. It also updates the IANA considerations of RFC 5939.

facts.label: New attributes
facts.value: rmcap, omcap, mfcap, mscap, lcfg, sescap

today: RFC 6871 is a Proposed Standard published in February 2013. It has not been obsoleted or updated, and it updates the IANA considerations of RFC 5939.

sections.title: Why Media Capabilities Need Negotiation
sections.content:
RFC 5939 gives SDP a general framework for indicating and negotiating capabilities, but the base framework only defines capabilities for transport protocols and attributes. RFC 6871 extends it with media capabilities that indicate and negotiate media types and their format parameters.

It also adds two things the base framework lacks. One is the ability to declare support for media streams that can be offered and negotiated later. The other is the ability to specify session configurations as combinations of media stream configurations. A real-life problem the RFC names is offering one stream (for example audio) while listing the ability to support another (for example video) without offering it at the same time.

The new attributes are chosen so that translating them into conventional SDP media attributes is straightforward. That simplifies the receiver's work: each proposed configuration is easy to turn into a normal media stream record, and an answer built from a chosen configuration is simple to construct.
sections.eli5: The old way let you say how you will talk, such as by phone or by letter. This new way also lets you say what language you speak and which topics you could talk about later.

sections.title: Actual, Potential and Latent Configurations
sections.content:
The RFC builds on three kinds of configuration, two of them from RFC 5939.

  • An actual configuration is ready to use in the current offer/answer exchange with no further negotiation. In an offer it is the base configuration, the ordinary m= line and its attributes.
  • A potential configuration is offered for possible use in the current exchange. It is an alternative that may be used instead of the actual configuration.
  • A latent configuration is neither ready for use nor offered. It only informs the other side of configurations the entity could support in a future negotiation.

A media capability, by itself, only indicates possible support. To actually use one in an exchange it MUST be referenced in a potential configuration.
sections.eli5: Actual is the dish already on your plate. Potential is the list of dishes you can swap it for right now. Latent is the list of dishes the kitchen could make another day.

sections.title: The New Capability Attributes
sections.content:
Media capabilities are numbered with media capability numbers, and the number is unique across the whole session description. They can be written at the session level or at the media level. A session-level one can be referenced by any pcfg or lcfg at the media level (consistent with the media type).

  • a=rmcap defines RTP-based media formats using a media subtype and its encoding parameters, such as PCMU/8000, without a payload type number. a=omcap defines non-RTP formats such as T38. A range of numbers lets one format carry different parameter sets.
  • a=mfcap attaches format parameters, normally those of fmtp, to one or more capabilities. Several mfcap lines for the same number are joined with ; in the order they appear, which keeps combinations of options compact. The existing acap attribute MUST NOT be used to encode fmtp attributes.
  • a=mscap attaches other media-specific attributes, such as rtcp-fb. A wildcard character after the number means the resulting attribute uses a wildcard in place of the payload type.

When a payload type number must appear inside a parameter, as with the redundancy format RED, an escape of the form %m= followed by a capability number and % is replaced by the payload type assigned to that capability.
sections.eli5: Each skill on your menu gets a number, like items on a lunch menu. Extra notes, such as 'no onions', are written next to the item number.

sections.title: Configuration Parameters and Latent Streams
sections.content:
Three new parameters are added to the configuration attributes. The m= parameter lists media capabilities, with alternatives separated by | in order of preference, most preferred first. The pt= parameter maps capability numbers to RTP payload type numbers, which is how the offerer can tell, for example, encrypted from unencrypted early media. The mt= parameter names the media type of a latent stream.

A latent configuration is written with a=lcfg. It is a media-level attribute that MUST include a media type (mt=) and a transport protocol parameter, and in most cases a media configuration too. Payload numbers are not assigned in a latent configuration, since that happens only if the stream is actually offered later. Latent configuration numbers do not imply a preference, and they MUST differ from potential configuration numbers. If keying material is needed to satisfy the format of a crypto attribute, the value MUST NOT be a real one and the receiver MUST ignore it.

The pcfg attribute gains the new parameters, and a potential configuration that includes media capabilities completely replaces the list of media formats on the m= line.
sections.eli5: The menu has a way to say 'my first choice, second choice' and a way to say 'I could also bring dessert later, but not today'.

sections.title: Session Capabilities and the Offer/Answer Exchange
sections.content:
Not every combination of configurations may be supportable, for example because of processing load or total bandwidth. The session-level a=sescap attribute lists acceptable combinations of configurations, each with a session number. A lower session number is preferred, and the session preference order takes precedence over the order in individual media streams. Square brackets mark optional configurations. If the answerer supports media capabilities negotiation and session configurations are offered, it MUST accept one of them or refuse the session.

An offerer that needs the extensions includes a=creq:med-v0. It writes the media capabilities, then potential configurations, optionally latent ones and sescap. The m= line carries the configuration to use if the other side does not understand capability negotiation, by default the least preferred. Config numbers MUST be unique in the whole SDP, which is stricter than RFC 5939.

The answerer checks that configurations are valid, picks the most preferred one it can support for each stream, and writes it as the answer's media line. It adds an acfg attribute naming the potential configuration used, and may add pcfg and lcfg attributes for other configurations it could accept, numbered as in the offer. Returned latent configurations MUST match the offered ones or a parameter subset. The answer's extra capabilities MUST NOT be used to build the base media description. The offerer then processes the answer as if it had offered those media capabilities, and later reconfigurations may reuse what it learned or exchange new capabilities.
sections.eli5: The host reads your menu, picks your favorite item they can cook, and tells you its number. If they do not understand your menu, they serve the plain meal listed first on the order form.

sections.title: Worked Examples
sections.content:
In the RFC's first example, Alice offers an audio stream with RTP and SRTP alternatives. The m= line offers plain RTP with PCMU or G.729B. Three pcfg lines list secure G.729 variants with telephone events first, then secure PCMU, then unsecured G.729B. Bob does not support SRTP, so he picks pcfg:3 and answers with a=acfg:3 m=4 t=2 pt=4:18 and a=csup:med-v0.

Other examples show six variations of the Adaptive Multi-Rate codec with different payload types, a session configuration that pairs G.711 mu-law with H.264 or G.729B with H.263-1998 for an endpoint with limited signal processing capacity, and latent configurations that announce future video and MSRP support while an audio stream starts. In the last one, the answer confirms the audio configuration and H.263 video, and the RFC notes that if congestion later becomes a problem, either party can offer a reconfiguration to G.729 to reduce packet sizes.
sections.eli5: Alice offers a few ways to talk, Bob says which one he can do, and they start talking that way.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The security considerations of RFC 5939 apply. The new risk is that latent configurations and sescap give attackers new things to tamper with. If an attacker can remove or alter latent configuration information to suggest that only non-secure or less-secure alternatives are supported, they may force a less secure session. An attacker who can insert or modify a sescap attribute may do the same, because its preference order overrides individual potential configuration order. The mitigations are similar to those in RFC 5939.

Middleboxes that control bandwidth, media flows or processing resources, but do not understand media capability negotiation, may be confused. The answer always carries the selected media encoding for every stream, so such a middlebox should examine the answer SDP to see the streams being established.
sections.eli5: If a sneaky person changes the menu so that only the unsafe options look available, you might end up with a less safe meal. So the menu must be protected from tampering.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content:
IANA registered the new SDP attributes rmcap, omcap, mfcap and mscap (session and media level), lcfg (media level) and sescap (session level). It added the option tag med-v0 to the SDP capability negotiation option tags registry from RFC 5939.

It also renamed and reshaped the registry of configuration parameters, with columns that say which RFC defines each parameter for potential, actual and latent configurations. The new registrations are m (media configuration), pt (payload type number mapping) and mt (media type), alongside the existing a and t. This is the sense in which the RFC updates the IANA considerations of RFC 5939.
sections.eli5: The names of the new menu words were written in an official list so everyone uses them the same way.

items.title: rmcap / omcap
items.text: Define RTP and non-RTP media formats as numbered capabilities.

items.title: mfcap
items.text: Adds format parameters, like fmtp, to capabilities.

items.title: mscap
items.text: Adds other media-specific attributes such as rtcp-fb.

items.title: lcfg
items.text: Announces a latent stream that is not offered yet.

items.title: sescap
items.text: Lists acceptable combinations of stream configurations.
